item.title: Scuffles break out and national anthems booed in Saudi-UAE football match
item.description:
Scuffles break out and national anthems booed in Saudi-UAE football match

Submitted by MEE staff on Wed, 10/07/2026 - 12:22
Fans throw bottles at UAE players, and Emirati fans appear to kick and shove Saudis outside stadium during ill-tempered Gulf Cup final
Saudi Arabia fans inside the stadium before the Gulf Cup final against the United Arab Emirates in King Abdullah Sports City Stadium, Jeddah on 6 October 2026 (Ibraheem Abu Mustafa/Reuters)
Off

Scuffles broke out between fans, and national anthems were booed amid an ill-tempered football match between the UAE and Saudi Arabia on Tuesday. 

The Saudis won 2-0 in Jeddah, claiming their first Gulf Cup title since 2004. 

The game got off to a tense start after sections of the Saudi fans jeered and chanted throughout the Emirati national anthem. The UAE goalkeeper was filmed shaking his head at the jeering.

Footage shared on social media appeared to show Emirati fans similarly singing loudly through the Saudi anthem. 

Other footage reportedly showed Saudi fans throwing bags towards Emirati fans. 

Also during the game, Saudi fans launched bottles at the Emirati players shortly before the final whistle. One UAE player was filmed launching a bottle back towards the fans. 

Those scenes came as referee Jalal Jayed issued three yellow cards for unsportsmanlike conduct, before giving a red card to UAE substitute Khaled Ibrahim, who had not even participated in the game. 

Saudi fans whistled and chanted through the UAE national anthem before the Gulf Cup final in Jeddah tonight.

UAE captain Khalid Eisa was visibly furious, reportedly mouthing "shame, by God, shame" during the anthem. pic.twitter.com/vvE749X7SV

— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 6, 2026

Ibrahim was sent off for shoving an assistant referee during a scuffle between both teams. 

Footage from outside the stadium appeared to show fans with Emirati flags draped around them throwing punches, and appearing to kick someone on the ground. Middle East Eye could not independently verify the footage. 

This is not the first time Emirati fans have been involved in violent scenes. 

In October last year during a World Cup qualifier match, UAE fans threw sandals, plastic bottles and cups at Qatari players who were celebrating scoring a goal. 

Some social media users linked Tuesday night’s tense scenes to wider tensions in the Gulf between Saudi Arabia and the UAE. 

For some time, the two powers have been at odds on issues ranging from oil production to the wars in Sudan and Yemen.

item.title: Israel marks third anniversary of 7 October Hamas attacks | First Thing
item.description:
Site of the Nova music festival near Re’im one of the locations where grieving relatives have gathered. Plus, the unlikely legal tussle over a ‘brain rot’ meme

Good morning. Israel is holding ceremonies and gatherings to mark the third anniversary of the 7 October attack by Hamas, in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken captive to Gaza. Israeli communities shattered by the massacres, torn between rebuilding their lives and remembering lost friends and relatives, have spoken to Emma Graham-Harrison about their experiences of that day and the days since. The Guardian is marking the day with a live blog, featuring the latest images of events taking place in Israel and around the world.

Israel’s government responded to the attack by launching a devastating war on Gaza, during which at least 74,243 people have been killed, according to the territory’s health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

What is happening with the flydubai attack investigation? New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation into the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound plane, after police confirmed he underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia. Disaster was narrowly averted on 30 September when passengers and crew intervened to stop the alleged attempt to take control of a flight to Tel Aviv with 182 people onboard.

What it is the latest settler violence? Armed Israeli settlers beat a photographer in the presence of Israeli soldiers, hospitalising him, as he covered worsening settler violence against olive farmers in the occupied West Bank. Jaafar Ashtiyeh, a 58-year-old veteran photographer for Agence France-Presse in Palestine, was beaten with the butts of rifles, despite him being marked as press, in view of about a dozen armed Israeli soldiers.

Who is the latest person taking legal action against the administration’s immigration enforcement? Marimar Martinez, a US citizen who was shot one year ago by a Customs and Border Protection agent during a sweeping immigration crackdown in Chicago, has filed a lawsuit against the federal government, alleging the agent lied about the shooting and fired into her vehicle from behind.

What has a whistleblower said about FBI investigations into LA anti-ICE protesters? Alex Padilla, a Democratic senator who represents California and serves on the Senate judiciary committee, said his office had received a copy of a complaint from a whistleblower that makes sweeping allegations about the Trump administration’s response to protests in LA in early 2025, claiming the president himself ordered the FBI to investigate protesters.

item.title: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say foreign warships have retreated from the Gulf
item.description:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards say foreign warships have retreated from the Gulf

Submitted by MEE staff on Wed, 10/07/2026 - 11:14
Brigadier-General Yadollah Javani said foreign military vessels were now located more than a 1,000km from Iran's shores
Members of Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps march during a military parade in Iranian capital, Tehran, in 2018 (AFP)
Off

An Iranian commander says the Revolutionary Guard’s military capabilities have forced foreign naval forces to keep their distance from Iran, according to state news agency IRNA.

Brigadier-General Yadollah Javani, deputy commander of the IRGC’s political bureau, attributed the shift in the Gulf and Sea of Oman to the force’s missiles, drones and naval strength.

“Previously, dozens of foreign warships and vessels roamed the Gulf,” he said.

“Today, the enemy’s fleet has moved more than 1,000km away from our territorial waters and does not dare approach.”

Javani said “collective security of Islamic countries and the complete withdrawal of the aggressors” would determine the region’s future.

Since the war started in February, Iran has established itself as the dominant military force over the Strait of Hormuz, which serves as the choke point for the rest of the Gulf region, which was traditionally known as the Persian Gulf but has been called the Arabian Gulf by Arab states in recent decades.

The region is crucial for world energy exports. Before the war, the strait carried roughly 20 million barrels per day (bpd) – a fifth of global daily oil consumption – with an estimated 10 to 14 percent of global supply remaining inaccessible six months on.

Iranian press review: Tehran says it will no longer wait to be attacked
Read More »

But shipments have almost returned to pre-war levels, thanks to backroom deals between Gulf states and Iran, and Tehran's own exports.

On Monday, US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said that 17 million barrels of oil transited the Strait of Hormuz on Monday.

Wright added that this marked the highest level of crude oil to pass through the waterway since the war on Iran disrupted shipping.

Nevertheless, securing control of the strait and negating Iran's influence on supply remains a key US strategic goal.

On Sunday, AP reported US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth saying the US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz is “ironclad” and that US President Donald Trump has “all the options he needs on the table” if Iran continues to “play games”.

“Iran wants to play games with things like the Strait of Hormuz. They don’t control it, we do,” Hegseth told reporters.

item.title: Houthis strike Yemen government and Saudi targets as violence intensifies
item.description:
Houthis strike Yemen government and Saudi targets as violence intensifies

Submitted by MEE staff on Wed, 10/07/2026 - 10:03
State media accuses Houthis of targeting airport in Aden, site of the internationally recognised government
A screen grab taken from video released by the pro-Yemeni government Southern Giants Brigades on 6 October 2026 shows fighting with the Houthis near the Bab al-Mandab Strait (Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP)
Off

Yemen's Houthis have hit a range of targets in Saudi Arabia and in pro-government areas including Aden, as the country's war intensifies.

According to the state-run Saba news agency, the Sanaa-based group targeted the airport in Aden, seat of the internationally recognised government, on Wednesday.

"Houthi terrorist militias targeted Aden International Airport with two ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones," the agency reported.

The Houthis, known officially as Ansar Allah, said they had targeted a military base located within the airport complex.

"Our armed forces fired ballistic missiles at a Saudi military supply convoy that had arrived at Camp Badr, near the airport," said Ansar Allah military spokesman Yahya Saree.

Earlier this week, Yemen’s internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, began a counter-offensive to retake Red Sea coastal territory that the Houthis captured last month.

The Yemeni government announced on Sunday that the campaign's overall objective is to retake all of the territory it has lost to the Houthis over 12 years of war.

Bab al-Mandab advance

Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies began attacking Houthi positions on Monday.

By evening local time, they claimed they had taken back the Arabian Gulf side of the Bab al-Mandab Strait and Mocha, the strategic Red Sea port city that the Houthis had wrested from them in September. 

Houthi channels denied that Mocha had been taken, posting videos of their fighters inside the city. Other reports and open source information appeared to corroborate this, suggesting that the fighting around the port city was largely made up of long-range missile exchanges and that Mocha remains in the hands of the Houthis.

Yemen: Video shows armoured vehicle ramming unarmed and armed men as fighting rages
Read More »

On Tuesday, the Iran-aligned movement claimed missile and drone attacks on several sites across Saudi Arabia.

Sanaa said it had targeted the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with drones. It also said that missile and drone strikes were launched at the Abha International Airport and an airbase in the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait.

The fighting in Yemen has intensified the humanitarian crisis in the country.

More than 130,000 people have been displaced inside Yemen since the beginning of August, the UN's refugee agency said on Tuesday. 

The UNHCR also reported that nearly 3,700 people had fled Yemen for Djibouti since 10 September. 

The World Health Organisation said 959 people were killed and 4,207 wounded across Yemen between 6 August and 2 October. 
 
The WHO also reported that cholera cases had tripled in three weeks, with 94 percent of recent cases recorded in five governorates hosting large numbers of displaced people, including Taiz, Aden and Abyan.
